segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For this Melchizedek—king of Salem, priest of God Most High, who met Abraham as he was returning from the defeat of the kings and blessed him,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and to whom Abraham apportioned a tenth of everything; who is first, by the translation of his name, king of righteousness, and then also king of Salem, that is, king of peace;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, but made like the Son of God—remains a priest for all time.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Consider how great this man is, to whom Abraham gave a tenth of the choicest spoils—the patriarch himself!

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now those of the sons of Levi who receive the priestly office have a command, according to the Law, to collect a tenth from the people—that is, from their brothers—even though they have come from the loins of Abraham.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the one whose genealogy is not traced from them has collected a tenth from Abraham and has blessed the one who has the promises.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And beyond all dispute, the lesser is blessed by the greater.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Here, people who die receive tenths; but there, it is one of whom it is testified that he lives.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And, so to speak, through Abraham even Levi, who receives tenths, has paid a tenth,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for he was still in the loins of his ancestor when Melchizedek met him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: If, then, perfection had come through the Levitical priesthood—for on the basis of it the people received the Law—what further need would there have been for a different priest to arise according to the order of Melchizedek, and not to be named according to the order of Aaron?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For when the priesthood is changed, there is necessarily a change of law as well.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the one about whom these things are said belongs to a different tribe, from which no one has served at the altar.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For it is plain that our Lord has sprung from Judah, a tribe about which Moses said nothing concerning priests.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And this is even more abundantly clear if a different priest arises in the likeness of Melchizedek,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: one who has become a priest not according to the law of a commandment concerned with the flesh but according to the power of an indestructible life.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For it is testified:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “You are a priest forever, according to the order of Melchizedek.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For on the one hand a former commandment is set aside because of its weakness and uselessness

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: (for the Law perfected nothing), and on the other hand a better hope is introduced, through which we draw near to God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And this was not without an oath. The others have become priests without an oath,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but he with an oath, through the one who said to him:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “The Lord has sworn and will not change his mind: ‘You are a priest forever.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: To that same degree Jesus has become the guarantor of a better covenant.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the others who have become priests are many, because death prevents them from remaining;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but he, because he remains forever, holds his priesthood permanently.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Therefore he is also able to save completely those who approach God through him, since he always lives to intercede for them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For such a high priest was indeed fitting for us: holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners, and raised higher than the heavens.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He has no need, as the high priests do, to offer up sacrifices day after day, first for his own sins and then for those of the people; for this he did once for all when he offered up himself.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the Law appoints as high priests human beings who have weakness, but the word of the oath, which came after the Law, appoints a Son who has been perfected forever.

notes.note: Melchizedek appears in Genesis 14:17–20, where he meets Abraham after a battle, blesses him and receives a tenth of the spoils. Otherwise he appears only in Psalm 110:4, which is quoted in verses 17 and 21. The whole chapter is an argument built on these two passages.

notes.phrase: without father, without mother, without genealogy
notes.note: Genesis records no parents, ancestry, birth or death for Melchizedek. Priestly office in Israel depended on documented descent, so the silence is striking, and the author reads it as a picture of a priesthood that neither rests on ancestry nor comes to an end. Most interpreters take this as an argument from what Scripture leaves unsaid; a minority think the author regarded Melchizedek as a heavenly being.

The Greek uses the ordinary word for “a tenth” and verbs formed from it throughout this passage. “Tithe” means the same thing and is the usual rendering, but the plain number keeps the link between Abraham’s gift in verses 2 and 4 and the Levites’ entitlement. The command referred to is in Numbers 18:21–28.

In Hebrews this word and the related verb in verses 19 and 28 speak of being brought to an intended goal, not of moral flawlessness. Here the goal is full and lasting access to God, as verse 19 indicates. Scholars differ on whether the word also carries an overtone of priestly consecration from its use in the Greek Old Testament.

notes.phrase: on the basis of it the people received the Law
notes.traditional: under it the people received the law
notes.note: The Greek preposition can mean “on the basis of” or “concerning.” On the first reading the Law given to the people rests on the priesthood as its foundation; on the second the Law simply contains regulations about the priesthood. The first fits verse 12, where a change of priesthood entails a change of law, and is the more common view.

notes.traditional: sprang out of Judah; was descended from Judah
notes.note: The verb is used of the sun or a star rising and of a plant sprouting, not normally of family descent. In the Greek Old Testament it and its related noun are tied to messianic images: the star rising from Jacob (Numbers 24:17) and the “Branch” of David’s line (Jeremiah 23:5; Zechariah 6:12). Many translations render it simply “descended,” which loses that echo.

notes.phrase: a commandment concerned with the flesh
notes.note: The adjective means “made of flesh” or “belonging to the flesh.” Most interpreters take it to refer to the rule that priests must be physical descendants of Aaron, and several translations paraphrase as “a requirement concerning bodily descent.” It may also suggest that such a rule belongs to the realm of what is mortal, in contrast to “an indestructible life.” It does not here mean sinful.

notes.traditional: Thou art a priest for ever after the order of Melchisedec
notes.note: Many later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, add “according to the order of Melchizedek” here. Several early witnesses lack the words, and they were probably added by copyists to match the fuller quotation of Psalm 110:4 in verse 17.

The word occurs only here in the New Testament. In period usage it means “permanent, inviolable,” and this is the sense standard lexicons give. Some interpreters, ancient and modern, take it as “not passing to a successor,” which fits the context well but is not clearly attested for the word.

The Greek phrase can express degree (“completely, fully”) or time (“for all time, forever”). Both fit the context, since the argument rests on Jesus living always, and the author may intend both. The traditional “to the uttermost” leans toward degree, as does the rendering here.

The sacrifice in which the high priest offered first for his own sins and then for the people’s belongs to the annual Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16), not to the daily service. The author may be combining that rite with the daily offerings as one picture of ceaseless sacrifice, or may mean that the high priest’s need recurred continually. Interpreters are not agreed.

candidates.reason: Central term across Hebrews, Paul and the Gospels where “covenant” and “will/testament” compete (notably Heb 9:16–17 and Gal 3:15), so a single policy is needed.

candidates.rendering: better (greater, of persons in rank, v. 7)
candidates.reason: A thematic word of Hebrews (better hope, covenant, promises, sacrifices) that translators vary between “better,” “superior” and “greater”; readers should see the thread.
Distinct from ἅγιος but usually rendered with the same English word; a decision is needed on whether to distinguish it (“devout,” “faithful”) across Acts, the Pastorals, Hebrews and Revelation.
The phrase εἰς τὸ διηνεκές recurs in Hebrews 10 and should be kept distinct from, yet consistent alongside, the “forever” used for εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα.

In Hebrews and 1 Peter it is a near-technical term for approaching God in worship, rendered variously “come to,” “draw near” and “approach,” and it needs to stay distinct from ἐγγίζω (“draw near,” v. 19).
